analysis.one_liner: Replaces the corporate income tax with a 14.5% business tax and cuts workers' payroll taxes in half.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 1994 with one Democratic cosponsor, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have eliminated the federal corporate income tax and replaced it with a 14.5% tax on the difference between a business's sales and its purchases. To offset the shift, it would have cut the Social Security payroll tax in half for both workers and employers, raised the standard deduction for low- and moderate-income taxpayers, and created a refundable tax credit for them that could be paid out through paychecks. It also applied the new tax to government-run services like public utilities, mass transit, and the postal service.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers would see their Social Security payroll tax rate cut from 6.2% to 3.1% on both the employee and employer sides, and the bill directs revenue from the new business tax into the Social Security trust funds to replace it. Low- and moderate-income taxpayers would get a much larger standard deduction (an extra $5,200 to $8,650 depending on filing status, phasing out above roughly $27,000–$45,000 of income) and a refundable tax credit that could be advanced through employers with each paycheck. Corporations would stop paying income tax entirely, though their dividends would be taxed as ordinary income to shareholders, and the new business tax would apply to their sales minus purchases.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the old-age, survivors, and disability insurance payroll tax by 50% for employees, employers, and the self-employed, and requires the Treasury to transfer a matching share of business activities tax revenue into the Social Security and disability trust funds.
Adds an extra standard deduction for low-income taxpayers, worth $5,200 for a single filer and $8,650 for a joint filer, phasing out as income rises above about $27,000 to $45,000.

Creates a refundable individual tax credit for low-income taxpayers, calculated at the 14.5% business tax rate on up to roughly $5,700 to $9,500 of income, with a mechanism for employers to advance it in paychecks.
Exempts businesses with gross receipts of $100,000 or less per quarter from the new business activities tax.
Excludes exports from the new tax, treating sales of property and services shipped out of the United States as tax-free.

analysis.who_pays: The 14.5% business activities tax would be levied on the gap between a business's sales and its purchases, which is largely value added; businesses would pass most of it through in the prices of goods and services, so consumers would bear much of it at the register. Government-run public utilities, mass transit systems, and the Postal Service would owe the tax on their operations, which could show up in utility bills, transit fares, or postage rates. Shareholders would give up the current lower tax rate on qualified dividends, since all corporate distributions would become ordinary income. The financing of Social Security would depend on the Treasury setting each year how much business-tax revenue to divert to the trust funds, replacing a dedicated payroll tax with a share of a new tax.

drawbacks.text: The business activities tax lands on consumption. Workers would get a payroll tax cut, but they would also pay the new tax embedded in everything they buy, and analysts of this type of tax design generally find that consumption taxes weigh more heavily on lower-income households, who spend a larger share of their income.

The bill would tax government-provided services: public utility services, mass transit services, and postal services would all be treated as taxable business activities, meaning transit agencies and utilities would owe 14.5% on fare and rate revenue net of their costs.

Repealing the corporate income tax removes a tax that falls substantially on the returns to capital held by wealthier households and by tax-exempt institutions; while the bill taxes dividends as ordinary income to shareholders, assets held through pensions and endowments would escape the corporate-level tax entirely.

Social Security's financing would shift from a dedicated payroll tax to an annual Treasury determination of how much business-tax revenue to credit to the trust funds, which the text leaves to the Secretary's judgment rather than a fixed formula.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was a serious, fully drafted attempt at trading one tax system for another: end the corporate income tax, roughly halve the worker-funded payroll tax, and raise the money with a broad tax on business value added, with refunds and credits aimed at shielding low-income households. The gains for workers and low-income filers were real and large, but the trade had genuine risks: a consumption-style tax tends to be regressive before the offsets, taxing utilities and transit directly reaches into household budgets, and Social Security would depend on Treasury discretion rather than a dedicated tax. The bill also left many details to Treasury regulations and required technical amendments to be supplied after enactment, so its true incidence was never fully pinned down.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on June 7, 1994, and the committee never took it up; the 103rd Congress ended four months later with the bill still sitting there.

narrative.text: Senator John Danforth, a Republican, introduced the bill on June 7, 1994, together with Senator David Boren, a Democrat, and delivered introductory remarks in the Senate over two days.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the day it was introduced.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed; the complete action history ends with the referral and introductory remarks.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, no one gained or lost directly; the existing corporate income tax and payroll tax simply continued, and the proposal's promised worker tax cuts and corporate tax repeal were both left untested.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The tax code stayed exactly as it was

for.name: Sen. John Danforth
for.role: U.S. Senator from Missouri; the bill's sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, delivered introductory remarks on it in the Senate on June 7 and 8, 1994, and saw it referred to the Finance Committee.

for.name: Sen. David Boren
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oklahoma; the bill's only cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Joined as cosponsor when the bill was introduced, making the initial sponsorship bipartisan.

against.name: Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the four months remaining in the Congress, leaving it to die in committee.

against.name: Sen. George Mitchell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor or sought a vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced jointly by a Republican and a Democrat, but with only two sponsors it never reached a stage where party positions could be measured; it died in a committee chaired by a Democrat without any recorded vote.

industries.note: Corporations would stop paying federal income tax entirely, but would owe the new 14.5% tax on sales minus purchases, and their dividends would become ordinary income to shareholders. Businesses with low labor costs or high purchase costs would fare far better than before; tax-exempt investors like pension funds would capture the full value of the repeal.

industries.industry: Retailers and other high-volume, low-margin businesses
industries.note: A tax on sales minus purchases hits labor-intensive businesses harder than ones that buy most of what they resell, since wages do not count as a deductible business purchase. Small businesses with quarterly receipts under $100,000 would be exempt entirely.

industries.industry: Government-run utilities, transit systems, and the Postal Service
industries.note: The bill treats public utility services, mass transit services, and postal services as taxable business activities, so these public providers would owe the tax on fare and rate revenue net of costs, pressure that would tend to reach riders and ratepayers.

The bill sets out detailed special rules taxing financial intermediation services through an allocation of fees and financial flows rather than ordinary receipts, and it excludes interest and life-insurance premiums from deductible business purchases, changing the effective burden on lending and insurance relative to the current income tax.
